For Heidegger, technology is not merely a collection of instruments, machines, or techniques, but a fundamental way in which beings are disclosed to human beings. In this sense, technology belongs to the history of truth, because truth is not simply the correctness of propositions but, in the Greek sense of aletheia, an unconcealment: a bringing-forth of what is out of hiddenness into presence. The Roman notion of veritas, which emphasizes correspondence and objectifying representation, narrows this broader disclosure into a more calculable and representational understanding of truth. Modern technology inherits this narrowed sense, but it also intensifies it by revealing reality in a distinctive historical mode. To say that technology is a human way of revealing is therefore not to say that humans freely invent a neutral tool, but that human beings are sent, or destined, into a particular way of encountering beings. Technology is “human” in the sense that it is the medium through which human existence discloses the world, yet it is not simply a product of human will; it is a destining, a Geschick, that gathers and directs how reality appears.

In modern technology, this revealing takes the form of what Heidegger calls Gestell, or “enframing.” Enframing does not create the world, but it challenges-forth nature and human beings to arrange themselves as standing-reserve, or Bestand. A river is disclosed not primarily as a river, but as a source of hydraulic power; a forest is disclosed as timber; land is disclosed as a site for development; even human beings are disclosed as labor-power or “human resources.” This is a genuine form of truth, because it unconceals a domain of availability, order, calculability, and efficiency. Reality becomes “more or less distinctly” standing-reserve because technology reveals beings as something that can be stored, optimized, and deployed. In this way, technology brings forth truth by making the world intelligible as a system of resources and functions. It also makes history accessible as an object for historiography, because the historical is represented as something that can be measured, classified, and controlled. Yet this very clarity is also a narrowing: what is revealed as standing-reserve is simultaneously what is concealed in its fuller, more primordial being.

The danger of modern technology, then, is not that machines are harmful in a simple instrumental sense, but that enframing becomes the exclusive way in which beings are disclosed. By revealing reality as standing-reserve, technology conceals other possible modes of truth, such as the bringing-forth of art, the self-emergence of physis, the silence of piety, or the openness of thinking. Heidegger’s point is therefore paradoxical: technology is a way of truth, but it is also a threat to truth because it reduces truth to objectifying representation. Nevertheless, because technology is a destining rather than a human invention, it contains within itself the possibility of a reflective response. Human beings are not the masters of technology, but they are the shepherds of its revealing. To understand technology as a mode of aletheia is to recognize that it discloses reality while also withdrawing other disclosures, and that our task is not to reject technology, but to stand within its truth in such a way that we remain open to a more primordial experience of being.

The passage from a modular mod-\(p\) representation to a modular \(p\)-adic representation is the modular lifting problem. Let \(E/\mathbb{Q}\) be semistable and let \(p>3\). The residual representation \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}:G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)\) is the reduction modulo \(p\) of the \(p\)-adic representation \(\rho_{E,p^\infty}\). If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is known to arise from a weight-2 newform, one must show that the full \(p\)-adic representation also arises from a newform; by the converse theorem for elliptic curves this would imply that \(E\) itself is modular. Wiles’s strategy is to encode all possible lifts of \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) satisfying the local conditions imposed by semistability in a universal deformation ring \(R\), and to encode all modular forms with the same residual representation in a Hecke algebra \(T\). The lifting theorem is then a comparison of \(R\) and \(T\): if the natural map between them is an isomorphism, or has the required surjectivity, every admissible lift is modular, in particular \(\rho_{E,p^\infty}\).

The comparison is difficult because \(R\) and \(T\) are defined by global conditions, and one must control their ranks and singularities. Wiles, following Taylor, introduced auxiliary primes \(q\) at which \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is unramified and whose Frobenius eigenvalues satisfy a prescribed congruence. Adding these primes enlarges the level and the deformation problem, but it makes the local deformation rings at \(q\) much simpler, often isomorphic to power series rings, and allows the Hecke algebra to be computed more explicitly. By choosing infinitely many such \(q\) and using a patching argument, one shows that the enlarged deformation ring and Hecke algebra have the same structure; then one removes the auxiliary primes to recover the original statement. This is the core of the Taylor–Wiles method, and it is what turns the abstract deformation-theoretic setup into a proof of modularity.

The reducibility of the residual representation determines which deformation-theoretic hypotheses are available. If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is irreducible, the universal deformation ring is local and its tangent space is governed by a Galois cohomology group \(H^1(G_{\mathbb{Q}},S,\bar{\rho})\), so the local-global comparison is relatively well behaved; irreducibility also prevents the representation from splitting into characters and ensures that the lift is controlled by the residual data. If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is reducible, it is an extension of two characters, and the deformation space can have several components or extra parameters. In that case the standard irreducible lifting argument may fail, and one must use additional arguments tailored to the reducible situation, often exploiting the special form of the characters and the semistable local conditions. For Frey curves arising from a putative Fermat counterexample, this distinction is essential: Wiles had to prove modularity in both the irreducible and reducible cases, with the reducible case requiring a separate treatment, before the contradiction with Ribet’s theorem could be completed.
